title: Verb + two objects
subtitle: I built my daughter a doll's house.
summary: Order the two objects after verbs like give and buy, choose between to and for, and spot the verbs that refuse one of the patterns.

lesson.heading: Two objects
lesson.text: Some verbs can be followed by two objects. Usually the first one (the **indirect object**) is a person or group of people, and the second one (the **direct object**) is a thing.

examples.text: Can you bring **me** *some milk* from the shops?
examples.note: me = indirect object, some milk = direct object

lesson.heading: Reversing the objects with for or to
lesson.text: With many of these verbs we can reverse the order of the objects if we put **for** or **to** before the indirect object (which then becomes a prepositional object).

examples.text: I built **my daughter a doll's house**. / I built **a doll's house for my daughter**.
Can you pass **me that bandage**? / Can you pass **that bandage to me**?

lesson.note: with for: book, buy, catch, choose, cook, fetch, find, get, make, order, pour, save. with to: award, give, hand, lend, offer, owe, show, teach, tell, throw.

lesson.heading: When the prepositional pattern is better
lesson.text: We use the pattern with *for* or *to* when we want to focus attention on the object that follows it, and when the indirect object is much **longer** than the direct object.

examples.text: Jasmin taught **music to a large number of children at the school**.
examples.wrong: Jasmin taught a large number of children at the school music

lesson.heading: Pronoun objects
lesson.text: If the direct object is a **pronoun**, the pattern direct object + preposition + indirect object is the usual one. Patterns without a preposition are avoided here because they are considered bad style.

examples.note: rather than I gave Isa them. / I gave them Isa.
rather than We bought them it. / We bought it them.

lesson.heading: to or for?

left.label: to = something is transferred to someone
examples: I hadn't got time to visit Mira, so I wrote a letter **to** her.
I sold him the car. (= I sold the car **to** him)

right.label: for = someone benefits from something
examples: Mira had broken her wrist, so I wrote a letter **for** her.
Jane posted the letter **for** me because I had flu.

lesson.note: Also bring, leave, pay, play, post, read, sell, send, sing, take. Sometimes the meaning is very similar: He played the piece to (or for) me.

lesson.heading: Verbs that cannot reverse their objects
lesson.text: Some verbs take two objects but can never turn the indirect object into a prepositional object with *for* or *to*.

examples.wrong: We all envied his lifestyle to him
Can I ask a favour to you

lesson.note: Also: allow, cost, deny, forgive, guarantee, permit, refuse.

lesson.heading: Verbs that need the preposition
lesson.text: Some verbs can only have a second object if it is a **prepositional** object - with *to* for the 'reporting' verbs, and with *for* for verbs like *fix*.

examples.note: but She told this joke (to me). or She told me this joke.
but I booked a room (for her). or I booked her a room.

lesson.note: with to: admit, announce, demonstrate, explain, introduce, mention, point out, prove, report, say, suggest. with for: collect, mend, repair.

lesson.text: Two pronouns? Put the thing first and the person after the preposition: I gave them to Isa, not ~~I gave Isa them~~.

exercises.prompt: Kaspar hates going shopping. I have to choose his clothes ___ him.
exercises.explanation: choose takes for: he benefits from what I do.

exercises.prompt: When Mr Durand bought the house, we sold all the carpets ___ him as well.
exercises.explanation: sell takes to when something is transferred to someone.

exercises.prompt: I'll be in late tonight. Can you save some dinner ___ me, please?
exercises.explanation: save is a 'for' verb: I benefit from the dinner being kept.

exercises.prompt: Which pattern does each verb allow?
categories: Both patterns: told me the joke / told the joke to me
Only with a preposition: described the situation to me

exercises.prompt: I can't reach the salt. Could you pass ___, please?
exercises.explanation: With a pronoun as the direct object we use direct object + to + indirect object.

exercises.prompt: He's got a very rewarding job. He teaches sports ___ disabled children.
exercises.explanation: teach takes to, and here the long indirect object goes at the end.

exercises.statement: He kindly collected me some library books.
exercises.explanation: He kindly collected some library books for me. collect can only have a prepositional object with for.

exercises.statement: I'd like to introduce you to my sister.
exercises.explanation: Correct. introduce needs a prepositional object with to.

options: Can I ask you a favour?
Can I ask a favour to you?
Can I ask a favour for you?
exercises.explanation: ask is one of the verbs whose objects cannot be reversed with to or for.

exercises.statement: He admitted his error for his colleagues.
exercises.explanation: He admitted his error to his colleagues. admit is a 'reporting' verb and takes to.

exercises.prompt: The clock on the wall was wrong. When we pointed out the problem ___ our teacher, she allowed us another half hour.
exercises.explanation: point out needs a prepositional object with to; allow, in contrast, keeps both objects (allowed us another half hour).

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. Remember that describe cannot take two plain objects.
exercises.answer: When he described his sister to me I didn't think I knew her
exercises.explanation: described his sister to me - not ~~described me his sister~~.
